paras: The killing of James M. Davis was the ambush shooting of a deputy United States revenue collector by a concealed party of men described as moonshiners, on the Beersheba road about three miles from McMinnville, Warren County, Tennessee, on the afternoon of March 13, 1882. Davis, known as a 'celebrated raider of moonshiners,' was shot from his horse and finished with shots to the head, and the papers reported between twenty and more than thirty bullet wounds. The federal revenue service offered rewards for the killers, but no arrest appears in the coverage.

Davis, about 35 and a native of Lincoln County, was a Confederate veteran who had joined the federal revenue service about eleven years earlier. He was credited with some 3,000 to 3,500 arrests and had killed several men in his work, including a man named Hampton near Winchester. According to a Nashville special, the moonshiners had made repeated attempts on his life, and the Nashville Banner reported that he had been warned two weeks earlier that men were lying in wait for him.

Davis and his men were returning from Beersheba Springs to McMinnville, with Thomas Vickers riding at his side and George Campbell and a man named Cathcart some distance behind. The attackers waited behind a breastwork of logs and cord-wood covered with cedar boughs about ten feet from the road, with the underbrush cut away to give a clear line of fire. The Nashville American later reported that a pistol shot from Ben Lomond Mountain had signaled the party's approach.

At the first volley Davis fell from his horse and Vickers fled; Davis rose and started back toward Campbell and Cathcart but was shot down again. Campbell's party saw one of the attackers come out and fire a pistol into Davis's head; another account said a shotgun. Davis reportedly fired three shots, and Campbell and Cathcart fired at the band before retreating to town. The attackers then left by a path over Ben Lomond Mountain.

The coroner summoned a jury and held an inquest at the scene, after which the body was brought to McMinnville and forwarded to Fayetteville for burial. Two wood-choppers, one white and one Black, whom the band had passed, told the coroner's jury they could not identify the men.

On March 14 Commissioner of Internal Revenue Green B. Raum telegraphed Collector W. M. Woodcock at Nashville to offer $300 for each assassin and to reinforce the marshal's posse. The Washington Evening Star reported a general belief in Tennessee that the reward was too small to secure arrests, and the Nashville American concluded that it would be very difficult to discover the men who killed Davis. No report of an arrest, indictment or trial was found.

The first reports came from a McMinnville special to the Nashville American, which the wires carried on March 14 to papers from Savannah and Memphis to Wheeling and Sacramento. Southern headlines treated the killing as an outrage against a brave officer: the Savannah Morning News ran 'Riddled with Bullets. Atrocious Murder in Tennessee,' the Memphis Daily Appeal 'A Brutal Crime,' and the Knoxville Daily Chronicle 'Assassinated!'

A National Associated Press dispatch printed in the Omaha Daily Bee under 'The Tennessee Terror' was harsher, saying Davis had more than half a dozen lives to answer for and had evaded several murder indictments. Distant papers in Maine and New Hampshire ran one-line items that put the killing on Saturday or Sunday evening. Tennessee weeklies, including the McMinnville Southern Standard and the Rugby Rugbeian, added biographies of Davis and the reward notices, and none of the coverage described the episode in racial terms.

The day of the killing varied: the local Southern Standard said 'Monday last,' matching the March 13 dateline of most wire copies, while the Savannah copy was datelined March 12 and the Rugbeian said Tuesday. Estimates of the attackers ran from eight to twenty, with the highest figure coming from Vickers, who fled at the first fire. The wire called Vickers Davis's companion, while the Evening Star and the Rugbeian called him Davis's prisoner, and the Rugbeian gave the reward as $200 each rather than the $300 in Raum's telegram.

reader.title: Killing of James M. Davis
bases: The papers describe the ambush killing of a federal revenue officer by a band of moonshiners on a road outside McMinnville, with no racial element reported and no claim of punishing a crime (A1, A4, A14).

Davis was killed without legal authority by a concealed party of eight to twenty men (A1, A11, A14, A15), but the papers present it as an assassination of a revenue raider by the moonshiners he hunted, motivated by their vows of revenge, not as punishment of an accused person under a pretext of justice, race or tradition (A7, A13).

The McMinnville special carried by the wires (A1, A2), a separate National Associated Press dispatch (A4) and the local Southern Standard (A14) independently agree on the ambush killing of Davis about two to three miles from McMinnville.

accounts.label: McMinnville special (wire)
accounts.gist: Davis was waylaid about three miles from McMinnville by a gang Vickers put at twenty, hidden behind cedar-covered logs; one ran out and shot him in the head, and his body bore over thirty bullet holes.

accounts.label: National Associated Press dispatch
accounts.gist: Davis, a 'special deputy United States marshal' on a raid, was ambushed two miles out, fired three shots, and was finished at close range while Campbell and Cathcart fired once each and retreated; the dispatch added that he had more than half a dozen lives to answer for.

accounts.label: Local weekly (Southern Standard)
accounts.gist: On Monday, returning from Beersheba Springs, Davis was shot from a log and cord-wood breastwork by 10 to 15 men, rose, and was killed by a second volley.

accounts.label: Nashville informant and coroner's-jury testimony
accounts.gist: Eight to twelve men, signaled by a pistol shot, let Davis and his prisoner Vickers pass before firing about 100 shots and escaping over Ben Lomond Mountain; wood-choppers who saw them could not name them.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Riddled with Bullets. Atrocious Murder in Tennessee', 'A Brutal Crime' and 'Assassinated!' framed the killing as an outrage against a celebrated officer.
The Omaha Bee's dispatch ('The Tennessee Terror') praised his bravery but said he seemed to 'take pleasure in hunting down his fellows' and had escaped murder indictments.
The Washington Evening Star relayed the revenue commissioner's tribute that he was 'as brave as a lion' and doubted the reward would bring arrests.
Distant papers ran one-line or one-paragraph wire items, some with wrong days of the week.
